beats.say: Everyday prices promise fairness. And they hide a discount illusion.
JCPenney says every tag is the final price, no coupons.
The same money buys the same items every day.
The one you can actually buy: the plain, unchanged price.
Sales fell 25% and the company lost $985 million. Sounds disastrous.
But it does a job: it sells the thrill of a discount.
By scrapping high-low sales, the store removed the visual cue shoppers love.
Without a sale tag, the everyday price feels like a steady bargain.
The $985 million loss proves the illusion collapsed.
You see it everywhere: a bakery lists a plain loaf $3, an artisan loaf $4, a premium loaf $7.
The artisan loaf becomes the smart choice because it feels like a deal for $4 versus $3 basic.
A gym does the same with a basic $20, a class pass $30, a premium $55; the class pass wins the mind.
Chase the feeling, not the price. Follow for more.
